relationship: named prophet and rebuilding leaders in the restoration narrative
rationale: Haggai's opening identifies Haggai, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak; Ezra names Haggai's prophecy and the rebuilding work of Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Iesous son of Iosedek. The parallel named participants are retained with each text's spellings.

relationship: second year of Darius as the setting for resumed temple work
rationale: Haggai dates his message to Darius's second year; Ezra says the Lord's house remained idle until that second year. The shared regnal year locates the appeal in the narrative's transition from halted work.

relationship: rebuilding delayed before the prophetic appeal
rationale: Haggai reports the people's claim that the rebuilding time has not arrived; Ezra records that work on God's house stood idle until Darius's second year. The narrative supplies the prolonged stoppage to which Haggai's appeal speaks, without equating external force with the people's stated excuse.

relationship: Haggai explicitly identified as the bearer of divine prophecy
rationale: Haggai introduces the Lord's word through the named prophet; Ezra explicitly identifies Haggai as prophesying to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in God's name. This links the named prophetic ministry, rather than merely two anonymous revelation headings.

relationship: contrast between a settled personal house and God's dwelling
rationale: Haggai challenges inhabitants of houses with recessed ceilings while God's house lies waste; David notices that he lives in a cedar house while God's ark remains in a tent. Both contrast domestic comfort with the condition of the divine dwelling, in different historical settings.

relationship: examination of one's way oriented toward the Lord
rationale: Haggai commands the people to set their hearts on their ways; Lamentations describes the way being searched and examined and calls for return to the Lord. Both connect reflection on conduct with a response toward God.

relationship: much sowing but little harvest and frustrated crop enjoyment
rationale: Haggai describes much sowing with little brought in and unsatisfied consumption; Deuteronomy's curse describes much seed with little gathered and denied enjoyment of wine and oil. The connection concerns agricultural futility, without assigning Deuteronomy's named pests to Haggai.

relationship: eating without satisfaction as covenant affliction
rationale: Haggai says the people ate without being satisfied; Leviticus warns of scarcity in which people eat and are not filled. Both treat food that fails to satisfy as an affliction.

relationship: same-chapter repetition of the command to examine one's ways
rationale: The command to place their hearts upon their ways repeats the earlier command to set their hearts upon their ways. The repetition frames the account of disappointing labor before the concrete rebuilding instruction.

relationship: procurement of timber for the Lord's house
rationale: Haggai directs the people to cut wood and rebuild the house; Ezra describes provision of payment and supplies to bring cedar timber for the rebuilding setting. Both join obtaining wood to the temple work, without identifying the mountain in Haggai with a specific place.

relationship: same-chapter return to the contrast between private houses and God's desolate house
rationale: Haggai attributes the reduced yield to His desolate house while people hurry to their own houses; the earlier challenge contrasts their finished ceilings with His wasted house. The repeated contrast makes the reason for the shortfall explicit.

relationship: withheld dew and produce contrasted with restoration
rationale: Haggai says heaven withholds dew and the earth its produce; Zechariah promises heaven's dew and the earth's produce to the restored remnant. The same two provisions are denied and then promised in the prophetic rebuilding setting.

relationship: withholding of dew announced by divine authority
rationale: Haggai announces heaven holding back dew; Elijah announces that no dew or rain will come apart from his prophetic word before the living Lord. Both make withheld dew an announced divine judgment, without equating the episodes.

relationship: the Lord bringing a sword as judgment
rationale: The native Haggai passage says the Lord brings a sword upon land, produce, people and labor; Leviticus warns that God brings a sword exacting covenant penalty. The correspondence preserves sword language rather than replacing Haggai's word with drought.

relationship: the named leaders respond to prophecy by rebuilding
rationale: Haggai says Zerubbabel, Joshua and the remnant listened to the Lord and Haggai; Ezra places the same leaders' beginning to build immediately after Haggai's and Zacharias's prophecy. The connection is the narrative response to prophetic ministry.

relationship: divine presence as the basis of encouragement
rationale: Haggai delivers the Lord's assurance 'I am with you'; Joshua receives courage because the Lord is with him wherever he goes. The shared assurance supports the work or task given in each setting.

relationship: God stirring people's spirits to build His house
rationale: Haggai says God stirred the leaders' and people's spirits and they worked on His house; Ezra says those whose spirits God stirred arose to go and build the Lord's house. Both attribute willing rebuilding action to God's initiative.

relationship: rebuilding undertaken by the named restoration leaders
rationale: Haggai records Zerubbabel and Joshua coming with the people to work on the Lord's house; Ezra records Zorobabel and Iesous beginning that house's construction with prophetic help. The common names and work establish the narrative parallel.

relationship: resumption of work within the specified second year of Darius
rationale: Haggai dates the work described immediately before this unit to the twenty-fourth day of month six in Darius's second year; Ezra ends the period of idle work at that same regnal year. Ezra supplies the year, not Haggai's exact month or day.

relationship: identified leaders of the temple rebuilding addressed again
rationale: Haggai's renewed instruction addresses Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak with the remnant; Ezra names Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Iesous son of Iosedek as the men beginning the rebuilding. The link identifies the addressed leaders in the construction narrative.

relationship: witnesses of the former house confronted with the new construction
rationale: Haggai asks those who saw the former glory how the present house appears; Ezra describes elders who saw the first house weeping as the new foundation is before them. Both make living memory of the first house important to the response to rebuilding.

relationship: strength and courage grounded in the Lord's presence
rationale: Haggai commands leaders and people to be strong and work because the Lord is with them; Joshua is commanded to be strong and courageous because the Lord is with him. The matching assurance undergirds action in each commission.

relationship: strengthened hands for the temple rebuilding work
rationale: Haggai tells the people and leaders to be strong and work; Zechariah tells hearers of the prophets at the founding and building of the temple to have strong hands. Both encourage the rebuilding community's labor.

relationship: the Lord's Spirit as assurance in Zerubbabel's building setting
rationale: Haggai assures the community that God's Spirit stands in their midst and calls for courage; Zechariah's word to Zerubbabel locates effectiveness in God's Spirit rather than great power or strength. The Spirit's presence or agency supports the work in both.

relationship: later citation of the promise to shake heaven and earth once more
rationale: Haggai promises once more to shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land; Hebrews quotes the promise to shake earth and heaven once more and reflects on the removal of shaken things. The explicit repeated wording establishes the citation relationship.

relationship: nations' valuable offerings and the glorification of God's house
rationale: Haggai says the nations' choice things will come and His house will be filled with glory; Isaiah describes nations' wealth, gold and offerings arriving, followed by the glorification of God's house. The relationship follows the native plural choice things rather than substituting a singular personal title.

relationship: all temple resources belong to God
rationale: Haggai declares silver and gold His; David acknowledges that everything given for God's house comes from God's own hand and belongs to Him. The surrounding temple donations include gold and silver, making the ownership statement materially specific.

relationship: the Lord's glory filling His house
rationale: Haggai promises greater glory for the house; Ezekiel sees the Lord's glory enter the house and fill it. The shared house-and-glory image does not establish that Ezekiel's vision is the exact building phase Haggai compares.

relationship: divine gift of peace extending to inner life
rationale: Haggai promises peace in the place and peace of soul for those building the sanctuary; Jesus gives His peace and tells the disciples not to have troubled or afraid hearts. The thematic parallel concerns inward peace as a divine gift, not identification of the builders with the disciples.

relationship: same-chapter date connecting the law inquiry and the turning-point exhortation
rationale: The oracle is dated to the twenty-fourth of the ninth month; the later instruction repeats that date as the day from which the people should direct their hearts. The repeated date connects the current message with its stated turning point.

relationship: priests charged to distinguish holiness and teach the law
rationale: Haggai asks the priests for a legal ruling; Leviticus charges the priests to distinguish holy from profane and clean from unclean and teach the Lord's statutes. This explains their role in the following holiness questions.

relationship: distinction between direct holy-flesh contact and indirect contact through a garment
rationale: Haggai's priests deny that food becomes holy when touched by the garment edge carrying holy meat; Leviticus calls the sacrifice most holy and says one touching its flesh is sanctified. The comparison carefully distinguishes direct contact with flesh from the mediated contact asked about in Haggai.

relationship: corpse contact as a source of uncleanness
rationale: Haggai asks about someone defiled through a dead person and the priests affirm resulting defilement on touch; Numbers says touching a dead person makes one unclean and explains the need for purification. This supplies the legal basis of the person's condition.

relationship: uncleanness transmitted by an unclean person's touch
rationale: Haggai's priests affirm that what a corpse-defiled person touches is defiled; Numbers explicitly says whatever the unclean person touches becomes unclean. This is the contact rule applied in Haggai's question.

relationship: hatred of rebuke at the gates
rationale: Haggai's expanded native reproof says the people hated those rebuking at the gates; Amos says they hated one reproving at the gates. The unusually particular phrase connects the two rebukes without omitting Haggai's wider defilement application.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between reflection before and from the rebuilding turning point
rationale: Haggai first asks the people to set their hearts on the time before stone was placed in the sanctuary; the later instruction asks attention from the stated day and the sanctuary's founding onward. The paired directions structure the before-and-after reflection.

relationship: same-book concrete illustration of reduced agricultural return
rationale: Haggai's reduced barley and wine measures specify the earlier complaint that much was sown but little brought in. The numerical shortfalls make the earlier agricultural futility concrete without changing the native units of measure.

relationship: divine agricultural blows failing to produce return
rationale: Haggai says God struck the people's labor with barrenness, wind damage and hail, yet they did not turn to Him; Amos describes burning, jaundice and devoured plantings, also followed by failure to turn. The shared rebuke concerns unheeded discipline, not identical agents of crop damage.

relationship: the temple foundation as a prophetic point of reference
rationale: Haggai directs attention from the sanctuary's founding and the named day; Zechariah addresses those hearing prophetic words from the day the Lord's house was founded. Both use the foundation as a reference point for the rebuilding community's response.

relationship: blessing replacing the former lack of agricultural fruit
rationale: Haggai asks about the still-unfruitful plantings and promises blessing from this day; Zechariah contrasts former treatment of the remnant with vine fruit, earth's produce and blessing. Both place renewed fruitfulness within a reversal from earlier want.

relationship: same-chapter second revelation on the earlier stated day
rationale: Haggai calls this a second word on the twenty-fourth day; the earlier heading specifies the twenty-fourth day of month nine in Darius's second year. The headings link the successive law-and-blessing and Zerubbabel messages within the chapter's dated sequence.

relationship: same-book repetition of the shaking announcement in the word to Zerubbabel
rationale: The renewed word to Zerubbabel repeats the shaking of heaven, earth, sea and dry land announced earlier to the rebuilding community. The repeated fourfold scope joins the final oracle to the earlier promise.

relationship: judgment in which a man's sword turns against his brother
rationale: Haggai says riders will fall with each one's sword against his brother; Ezekiel announces a man's sword against his brother as part of God's judgment. The precise fraternal combat image supports the parallel without equating the armies.

relationship: God's sovereignty over the removal of kings
rationale: Haggai promises to overturn royal thrones and destroy kings' strength; Daniel says God transfers kings and appoints them. Both place royal power under God's authority to remove it.

relationship: contrasting treatment of a named Judean figure through signet imagery
rationale: Haggai promises to make the chosen servant Zerubbabel like a signet; Jeremiah says Jeconiah would be pulled off even if he became a signet on God's right hand. The shared signet image is used for selection in one and removal in the other, without resolving all dynastic implications.
